intro.title: Guide
intro.subtitle: Every feature, mode and variant in the app, and the small rules that are easy to miss. Tap a topic to open it.
intro.versionText: Version %1. Rules that the server operator can change — ranked categories, their boards and time limits — are described here but shown live on the Ranked Duel panel.

topics.title: How Minesweeper works
topics.summary: Reveal every safe cell without setting off a mine.

items: The board is a grid of hidden cells and some of them hide mines. Reveal a cell and it shows a number: how many of the cells touching it are mines. A cell touching no mines at all shows nothing and opens its neighbours for you, which is why one click can clear a whole region at once.
You win when every safe cell is revealed. You do not have to flag the mines — flags are a note to yourself, not a win condition.
Flags never explode. A flag is the only thing you can put on a cell you believe is a mine, and placing one is always safe.

The first reveal is always safe. The board is not generated until you click it, and it is then built around your click — usually with its neighbours cleared too, so the first click opens a region. PVP Conquest is the exception: it generates the whole board up front, without a safe zone.
The mine counter counts flags, not mines. It shows the mine count minus the flags you have placed, so over-flagging drives it below zero. It is never a hint about whether your flags are right.

topics.title: The board screen
topics.summary: Mine counter, timer, pause, and the buttons that only appear sometimes.

items: Left: mines remaining. Middle: the pause button, whose face reflects the state of the round. Right: the timer.

The 👆 / 🚩 button next to the mine counter switches what your Primary action does. It only appears if at least one of your click mappings is set to Primary or Secondary — if none are, there is nothing for it to switch and it stays hidden.

Zoom and re-frame buttons appear only on devices that have no other way to do it. A mouse has a wheel and a touchscreen has a pinch; a TV remote has neither, and its D-pad is already spoken for by the cell selection.
Pause opens the in-game menu, which is also where Back takes you during a round. In online modes the round does not stop while you are in there.
Other players' names appear on shared boards, and action decals mark the cell each player just revealed or flagged. Duels deliberately suppress decals — you are not meant to watch your opponent play.

topics.title: Chording
topics.summary: Hold a number to open all of its remaining neighbours at once.

items: Hold on a revealed number and the cells it would open are previewed. Release and, if you have already flagged as many neighbours as the number says, every other neighbour is revealed in one go. It is the fastest way to clear a board once the flags are down.
Chording trusts your flags. If one of them is wrong, chording reveals a mine and you die. It is a shortcut, not a safety check.
It works in every variant — the flat board, the 3D box, the endless grid, custom levels. It is a capability of the cell you are pressing, not a feature of one board type.

On a touchscreen it shares the long-press gesture. Holding a hidden cell does whatever Long Press is mapped to; holding a revealed number chords. The two never collide because a cell is either revealed or it is not.
Turn it off in Settings → Controls → Gestures if you would rather a hold always mean the same thing.

topics.title: Click mapping
topics.summary: What left click, right click and long press each do.

items: Settings → Controls → Input Mapping gives each of the three gestures its own action: Reveal, Flag, Primary, Secondary or None.
Reveal / Flag always do that one thing.

Primary / Secondary follow the 👆 / 🚩 toggle on the board: Primary does whatever the toggle currently shows, Secondary does the other one. This is what makes one-finger play work — one gesture, switched deliberately.
None disables the gesture entirely.
R always reveals and F always flags, whatever the mapping says. The keyboard shortcuts are fixed on purpose, so there is always a way to do both.
Arrow keys and the D-pad move the cell selection, and Enter or OK acts on it as a left click. Holding Enter or OK counts as a long press.

topics.title: Press and hold
topics.summary: Enable it, map it, and set how long a hold has to be.

items: Long press is off until you enable it, and it has its own mapping row once you do.

Long Press Duration sets how long the hold has to last. The default is chosen for the device you are on — a remote or a touchscreen wants a longer hold than a mouse — and Reset puts that default back.
The hold is timed by the board itself, so the same duration applies whether you are holding a mouse button, a finger, Enter or the OK button on a remote.

topics.title: Panning, zooming and the 3D box
topics.summary: Moving the view without accidentally playing a move.

items: Zoom with the wheel, a pinch, Ctrl and +/−, or the shoulder buttons on a controller.
Pan by dragging. Whether a plain one-finger (or left-button) drag pans is a setting: with it off, a drag on the board is treated as a click on the cell you started on.
Three or more fingers always pan, whatever that setting says, so there is always a gesture that cannot be mistaken for a move.
The 3D box orbits instead of panning: one finger orbits, two fingers zoom and orbit together, three or more orbit only.

topics.title: Follow selection
topics.summary: Whether moving the selection brings the view with it.

items: When you move the cell selection with the arrow keys or a D-pad, the view can follow it: Never, only when the board does not fit on screen, or Always.

The 3D box is a special case. Half of it is hidden behind itself at all times, so it follows the selection unless you have chosen Never — otherwise the selection would routinely be somewhere you cannot see.

topics.title: Controller, D-pad and TV
topics.summary: The whole app is playable without a pointer.

items: Every screen can be driven with a D-pad. The focused control is drawn with a ring around it; OK activates it and Back goes up one level.
On the board, the D-pad moves the cell selection rather than jumping between buttons — the board takes the D-pad over while it is focused.
Back during a round opens the pause menu instead of leaving the game, so a stray press never drops you out of a match.

Directional movement picks the neighbour that is genuinely in that direction. A control that only touches the corner of what you are on is not treated as adjacent, which is what stops a full-screen board from swallowing every direction at once.

topics.title: Levels, categories and progress
topics.summary: Preset boards per variant, grouped into categories.

items: Solo Play opens on a row of variants: Minesweeper, 3D, No Guessing, Fog of War, Infinite and Custom. Each has its own set of preset levels grouped into categories.
A level card shows the board size and mine density, your stars, and your best time. A category shows how much of it you have completed.
Solo play needs no connection at all. Completions are stored on this device and on your account, so they follow you to another device — see Account and data.
Levels can also be started straight from the Achievements page, which launches the exact preset an achievement is asking for.

topics.title: Stars and best times
topics.summary: Three stars per level, scored on time — and they can move.

items: ★1 is any completion, however slow. ★2 and ★3 are time bars set per level.
Only your best time is stored. Nothing anywhere records a star count — stars are recalculated from that time every single time they are shown.
That has a consequence worth knowing: if a level's time bars are re-tuned, your stars move, up or down, without you playing a game. Your recorded time is never touched.
The stars you see are the better of your time on this device and the best time on your account.

topics.title: Rated levels and the leaderboard
topics.summary: Which runs are submitted, and why a fast one can be refused.

items: Some presets are rated. Clear one while connected and your time is submitted; the result screen then shows your placement, or tells you the run was recorded but did not reach the top times.
Custom sizes and the local-only variants are never rated — there is no shared board to compare them on.

The server refuses times that are far below a level's ★3 bar, because no honest run gets there. Small boards are exempt: on a tiny grid an opening cascade really can clear almost everything at once, and honest players were losing those runs.
Rated runs are also recorded as replays — see below.

topics.title: Custom games and Continue
topics.summary: Your own board size, and the one saved game per variant.

items: Every variant has a Custom entry where you set width, height, density and whatever else that variant needs — length for 3D, visible cells for Fog of War, the solver mode for No Guessing.
One unfinished custom game is kept per variant, and Continue Last Game resumes it exactly where you left off.
Starting a new custom game, or changing the custom settings, erases that saved game. You are asked to confirm first, because it is easy to walk into while browsing the sliders.

topics.title: Replays
topics.summary: Watch a leaderboard run move by move.

items: Rated solo runs are recorded. On the leaderboard, WATCH plays one back.

A replay stores the board's seed and your moves, not the board. The board is rebuilt from the seed before playback, which is why the very first move is watchable and why the board behaves like a real board rather than a slideshow.
Extremely long games stop recording at a limit. If you are watching one of those, the viewer tells you the recording is only the start of the run.

topics.title: Normal
topics.summary: Classic 2D Minesweeper. Online and rated.

items: A flat rectangular grid where each cell touches up to eight neighbours. This is the variant every game mode supports, and it has leaderboards.

topics.title: 3D — the cuboid
topics.summary: The six outside faces of a box, stitched together at the edges.

items: You play the surface of a width × height × length box, not its inside. The cell count is therefore 2·(w·h + w·l + h·l) — a long thin box has far more cells than its longest side suggests.

Adjacency wraps across the edges. A number on a face counts neighbours that live on the face around the corner from it, which is the whole difficulty of the variant: an edge cell's neighbourhood is not what a flat board trained you to expect.
You orbit the box rather than panning it, and half of it is always facing away from you. That is why the view follows your selection here unless you have explicitly set Follow Selection to Never.
Online and rated, including as a ranked duel category.

topics.title: Fog of War
topics.summary: Only your most recent reveals stay visible.

items: The board remembers only the last N cells you revealed, where N is the level's visible cells parameter. Reveal something new and the oldest visible cell falls back into the fog.

The cells are still revealed — the board underneath does not change and you never have to re-clear anything. What you lose is the sight of them, so it is a memory variant rather than a harder-board variant.
Online and rated, and available as a ranked duel category. It is the one variant PVP Conquest cannot use: capture depends on seeing what has been taken, and fogged reveals cannot drive that.

topics.title: No Guessing
topics.summary: Boards generated so that logic is always enough.

items: The board plays exactly like a normal one — same geometry, same cascade, same win condition. The difference is entirely in how the mines are placed: a solver checks the layout and the generator keeps looking until it finds one you can actually solve.
Deterministic: every single step is forced by certain deduction. You never have to take a risk.

No coinflip: pure 50/50s and n-way ties are forbidden, but a position with one clearly least-risky move (33% against 66%, say) is allowed. It uses the global mines-remaining count, not just the numbers next to you — so counting the mines you have left is part of the variant.

The board is generated after your first click, and finding a solvable layout is real work. On a big or dense board there can be a short pause between that first click and the board appearing. It runs off the main thread so the app stays responsive while it searches.
Online and rated, and available as a ranked duel and conquest category.

topics.title: Infinite
topics.summary: An endless grid with a score instead of a win.

items: The grid has no edges and is generated as you go, so there is nothing to complete. Your score is the number of safe cells you have revealed, and your best is kept per density.
One mine ends the run. There is no clearing it and no leaderboard placement — it is a personal high-score chase.
Local only. Infinite cannot be hosted online and has no server leaderboard, though it does count towards your statistics and achievements.

topics.title: Custom levels
topics.summary: Draw your own board shape, then play it.

items: The level builder lets you mask cells out of a large grid, so the board can be any shape you like rather than a rectangle. Set the density, save it, play it.
Cells you masked away are not part of the board at all: they are never mines and never count towards completion.
Local only, like Infinite — your levels live on this device and cannot be hosted online or submitted to a leaderboard.

topics.title: Lobbies, hosting and joining
topics.summary: How an online game gets started.

items: Create Online Lobby lets you pick the mode, the variant and the board, and whether the lobby is public or private. Game Browser lists the public ones.
Private lobbies are reached by invite. A friend can be invited straight from the Friends page or from inside the lobby.
Who restarts depends on the mode: the host does in co-op and solo lobbies, competitive modes wait for everyone to be ready, and Community never restarts at all — you respawn instead.
Joining a round already in progress is allowed in the co-op modes and Community. Competitive modes seat you for the next round.
Ranked play has no lobby. It is matchmaking only, from the Ranked Duel panel.
Leaving a game or lobby returns you to the screen you started it from, not to the main menu.

topics.title: Freeze time at the start of a round
topics.summary: A short countdown where actions are refused.

items: Every online round opens with a freeze — about a second in co-op and solo lobbies, about three in the competitive modes — so that everyone is looking at the board before anyone can touch it. Actions sent during the freeze are refused.

All timing is anchored to the end of the freeze, not to the moment the round message arrived. The timer on your screen, the time on the leaderboard and the time-alive in your statistics therefore always agree, whatever your connection did. Community is the one exception: there, your clock starts on your own first reveal.

topics.title: Co-op Hardcore
topics.summary: One shared board, up to 8 players. One mine ends it for everyone.

items: Everyone plays the same board at the same time and clears it together.
Any mine ends the round for the whole lobby — that is the hardcore part. The mines are revealed and the result screen opens for everybody.
Join mid-round and you are alive immediately and can play at once.
A board cleared by the group counts both as a grid you completed and as one your team completed, which are tracked separately in statistics.

topics.title: Co-op Softcore
topics.summary: One shared board, up to 8 players. A mine kills only you.

items: The same shared board, but hitting a mine kills only you. Everyone else keeps playing and you watch — their board stays alive.
When you die, the board is revealed to the lobby's players so the survivors are not held back.

Join a round whose board has already been generated and you start dead, spectating until the host restarts. Join before the first click and you are in properly. This is the opposite of Hardcore and catches people out.

topics.title: Community
topics.summary: One enormous public board, up to 64 players, always running.

items: A single public board that everyone shares and that nobody hosts. There is no start and no restart: you join whatever is in progress.
Your clock starts on your own first reveal, not when you joined — the only mode where that is true, because a shared permanent board has no round start to measure from.

Hit a mine and you are out until a respawn cooldown expires (half an hour by default). You can leave and come back; the cooldown is remembered. Turn on the respawn notification in Settings → General to be told when it is up.
Your flags are yours alone. They are never sent to anyone else's board — but they still count towards your score.

Score: 3 points per cell you reveal, 2 per flag you place, plus a finishing bonus worth 1% of the whole board to whoever reveals its last cell. The board's placements are kept, so first places and top-three finishes appear in your statistics.
Idle players are removed from the board to keep the slots circulating, and your name is only attached once you actually do something.

topics.title: PVP Duel
topics.summary: Two players, two identical boards, one race.

items: You each get your own copy of the board and race to clear it. Your opponent's moves never touch your grid and yours never touch theirs.
Hitting a mine ends the round for you immediately.
Live reveal and flag totals for both players are tracked, and the pause screen shows how the two of you compare while the round is still running.
Action decals are suppressed here — you should not be able to read your opponent's play off your own board.

topics.title: PVP Teams
topics.summary: Teams race on a board each; deaths do not end it.

items: Each team gets its own board and races to clear it. A mine kills the player who hit it — the team's board stays alive and their teammates carry on.
When your player dies, your own team's board is revealed to you. Other teams' boards are not.
If every team is wiped out, the team that had revealed the most cells wins. Equal top totals are a genuine tie, not a coin toss.
Ready needs both teams to have players in them, so a round cannot start with one team empty.

topics.title: PVP Conquest
topics.summary: One shared board where cells belong to whoever revealed them.

items: Conquest is the odd one out: a single board that everybody plays at once, where the point is not to clear it but to own more of it than anyone else.
Your first reveal must be within three cells of an edge of the board. Everyone starts from the outside and works inwards.
After that you can only reveal a cell next to one you already own. Your territory grows outwards from where you landed; you cannot jump to a nicer-looking corner.
Flags follow the same rule — you can only flag next to your own cells, and you can only remove your own flags. Someone else's flag is not yours to clear.
Hitting a mine does not end the board. The real way to lose is to be blocked: no legal move left anywhere on your frontier.
The winner is whoever conquered the most cells when nobody can move. Ties are real results and are reported as such.
Your moves are applied on your screen the instant you make them and quietly corrected if the server saw it differently, so the board feels immediate on a slow connection.
Because the whole board is generated up front, there is no safe zone around anyone's first click. Conquest also cannot be played on Fog of War.

topics.title: Ranked Duel and Ranked Conquest
topics.summary: Matchmade 1v1 with an ELO rating per category.

items: No lobby. You pick a category on the Ranked Duel panel and queue; the server pairs you. The panel shows each category's board, its first-to target and its round time limit.
You start at 1200, and your rating is separate for every category. Before you queue, the panel previews exactly what a win, a draw and a loss would do to it.

The search widens as you wait. It starts by looking for opponents very close to your rating and steps the window open the longer nobody turns up, so a quiet category still finds you a game — just a less even one.
A match is first to N rounds. Rounds that hit the time limit are decided on cells revealed, and are drawn if those are equal too.
Forfeiting and offering a draw are allowed in ranked matches, and both count as real results.
Ranked Conquest is the same structure over a shared conquest board, except that cells are owned by player rather than by team.
You can also challenge a friend directly into a ranked category from the Friends page.

topics.title: Statistics
topics.summary: Per mode and per variant, tied to your account.

items: The Statistics screen has a tab per mode — plus Total, Online Total, Solo and Solo Rated — and each can be narrowed to a single variant.

You get an overview (games, time alive), results where the mode has them (wins, losses, win rate), board activity (reveals, flags, mines clicked) and progress (grids completed by you and by your group).
Community adds placements: first places and top-three finishes.
Online statistics are counted by the server, not by your client, and they live on your account — so they are the same on every device you play on and cannot be inflated locally.
Time alive uses the same anchor as everything else: it starts when the freeze ends.

topics.title: Achievements
topics.summary: Milestone tracks plus one per preset level.

items: Milestones track a counter — cells revealed, flags placed, games won and so on — across escalating thresholds worth one, three or five stars. Some count everything, some count only solo play, some count a single mode or a single variant.
Level achievements are one per preset level, always three stars, scored on your best time. They are the same stars the level card shows.
The page can be filtered and each level achievement can start that exact level for you.
Achievements are held on your account and synced when you open the page, so unlocking something on one device shows up on the others.

topics.title: Leaderboards
topics.summary: Best times per level, and ELO rankings per ranked category.

items: Pick a variant and a level to see its best times, paged; your own entry is pinned so you can always see where you are.
WATCH plays a run back as a replay. STATS opens that player's profile — their statistics, their ranked ratings and their achievement counts.
The ELO view ranks players per ranked category, with wins and losses.
▶ Rated starts the level you are looking at, so a leaderboard is also a way to launch a run at it.

topics.title: Screenshots
topics.summary: Turn a finished board into a shareable image.

items: The camera button on the end-of-game screen composes your board and the result into a single image at a fixed shape — landscape or portrait depending on the board — at 1080p or better.
Shots are kept in a local gallery reachable from the Statistics header, where they can be viewed, shared or deleted.
On Android, sharing and saving need no permissions at all — the image is handed to the system rather than written into your photo library behind your back.

topics.title: Friends, friend codes and blocking
topics.summary: Add people by their numeric code.

items: Everyone has a friend code, shown on the Friends page and in Settings → Account. Add someone by typing theirs; you cannot add yourself, and you have to unblock someone before you can befriend them.
The friends list shows presence: offline, online, in a lobby or in a game.
Recent players and your private notes are stored on this device only. They are a memory aid, not part of your account, and they do not travel to another device.
Blocking someone stops their invites and hides them from you. Names can change, so the list shows the current name for a code you already know.

topics.title: Invites and challenges
topics.summary: Pull a friend into your lobby, or duel them directly.

items: Invite a friend to the lobby you are in, or send them a ranked challenge in a category of your choice — that skips the queue and puts the two of you straight into a rated match.
Who may invite you is up to you: Nobody, Friends only, or Anyone (Settings → General → Notifications).
Invites have a short cooldown so they cannot be used to pester someone.

topics.title: Chat and announcements
topics.summary: Talking in a lobby, and messages from the server.

items: Lobbies have a chat panel. Pop-up notifications for new messages can be turned off in Settings → General.
Names and messages are filtered; a name containing banned words is refused at registration rather than quietly renamed.
On Android the chat input lifts itself above the on-screen keyboard and grows to three lines before it starts scrolling.
Server announcements appear as a banner — scheduled messages from whoever runs the server, about maintenance or events.

topics.title: Your account and your devices
topics.summary: One account, several devices, joined by a transfer phrase.

items: There is no password and no e-mail. This device holds an account, created the first time it connected, and several devices can share one.

To add a device: create a transfer phrase on a device that already has the account and type it into the new one's Account tab. The phrase adds exactly one device, expires after ten minutes, and works for anyone who has it — so keep it to yourself.

The Account tab lists every device on the account with when it was last seen and how it got there. Remove signs another device out; it gets a fresh account next time it connects, and any unused transfer phrase is invalidated.
Leaving the account on this device wipes this device's achievements, statistics and completed levels and starts it over with a new account. Your other devices keep everything.

topics.title: What is stored where
topics.summary: Device data, account data, and what the erase buttons really do.

items: On this device: your settings, saved custom games, custom levels, screenshots, recent players and friend notes.
On your account: completed levels and best times, achievements, and all online statistics.
Delete Solo Progress On This Device clears the local copy only. Levels recorded on your account come straight back the next time this device syncs — that is not a bug, it is where they live.

Erase Level Progress From Account removes completed levels and best times everywhere, on every device, while keeping achievements and lifetime statistics. A device that is offline and still holding its own local progress will upload it again when it next connects, so erase from a device that is connected.
Reset All Settings only touches settings. It never touches progress.

topics.title: Offline, servers and versions
topics.summary: What still works with no connection.

items: Solo play works completely offline, including levels, custom games and the local variants. Progress is banked and syncs when you reconnect.
Online modes, leaderboards, ranked play, friends and achievement sync all need a connection.
The server address can be set by hand in Settings → System, and Re-fetch asks for the current official address again if you have pointed it somewhere else.
Client and server versions must be compatible. If yours is too old the server says so at connection time rather than letting you into a game that would misbehave.
When the server is in backup or maintenance mode some features are unavailable and say so.

topics.title: Theme, size, density and language
topics.summary: Four separate knobs for how the app looks.

items: Theme — Dark, Classic Blue or Soft Light. UI Size scales the text and controls from Micro to Big. Density squeezes the padding between them.
Size and density are independent on purpose: Big and Very Compact together give you large text with very little space around it, which is what a small phone in landscape actually wants.
Language follows your system by default and can be pinned to any shipped language. Switching retranslates the app in place — no restart.

topics.title: Board themes
topics.summary: How the board itself is coloured, including your own.

items: The board has its own theme, separate from the app theme, and the tiles in Settings → Appearance are live previews rather than pictures.
Custom opens an editor where every part of the board — cells, numbers, flags, grid lines — is yours to set. Changes show up on the previews immediately.
The board theme is per device, not per account.

topics.title: Sound, decals and notifications
topics.summary: The small switches and what they actually control.

items: Flag and reveal volumes are separate, because on a big cascade the reveal sound is doing much more work than the flag one.
Action decals mark the cell each player just revealed or flagged so a shared board shows who did what. Duels ignore this setting and never show them.

Keep lobby connected while backgrounded (Android) stops you dropping out of a lobby when you switch apps. It may ask for a permission, and the switch follows what the system actually granted rather than what you tapped.
Notify me when I can respawn schedules a local notification for the end of a Community cooldown. It is scheduled on the device, so it works whether or not the game is running.
On Android, game sound is quiet during a phone call — the system reserves the audio for the call.
